<title>Californium</title>
<fragment>

</fragment>

</fragment>
<fragment>

1. **^**  The Earth formed 4.5 billion years ago, and the extent of natural neutron emission within it that could produce californium from more stable elements is extremely limited.
2. **^** A double hexagonal close-packed (dhcp) unit cell consists of two hexagonal close-packed structures that share a common hexagonal plane, giving dhcp an ABACABAC sequence.[15]
3. **^** The three lower-mass transplutonium elements—americium, curium, and berkelium—require much less pressure to delocalize their 5f electrons.[17]
4. **^** Other +3 oxidation states include the sulfide and metallocene.[18]
5. **^** Europium, in the sixth period directly above element 95, was named for the continent it was discovered on, so element 95 was named americium. Element 96 was named curium for Marie Curie and Pierre Curie as an analog to the naming of gadolinium, which was named for the scientist and engineer Johan Gadolin. Terbium was named for the village it was discovered in, so element 97 was named berkelium.[33]

</fragment>

35. **^** Diamond, H.; Magnusson, L.; Mech, J.; Stevens, C.; Friedman, A.; Studier, M.; Fields, P.; Huizenga, J. (1954). "Identification of Californium Isotopes 249, 250, 251, and 252 from Pile-Irradiated Plutonium". *Physical Review*. **94** (4): 1083. Bibcode:1954PhRv...94.1083D. doi:10.1103/PhysRev.94.1083.
36. **^** "Element 98 Prepared". *Science News Letter*. **78** (26). December 1960.

</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Prices of chemical elements</title>
<fragment>

As of 2020[update], the most expensive non-synthetic element by both mass and volume is rhodium. It is followed by caesium, iridium and palladium by mass and iridium, gold and platinum by volume. Of those elements, rhodium, caesium and gold have only one stable isotope (133  
Cs, 103  
Rh and 197  
Au respectively), iridium has two (191  
Ir and 193  

</fragment>
<fragment>
Ir) whereas palladium and platinum both have several. Carbon in the form of diamond can be more expensive than rhodium. Per-kilogram prices of some synthetic radioisotopes range to trillions of dollars. While the difficulty of obtaining macroscopic samples of synthetic elements in part explains their high value, there has been interest in converting base metals to gold (Chrysopoeia) since ancient times, but only deeper understanding of nuclear physics has allowed the actual production of a tiny amount of gold from other elements for research purposes as demonstrated by Glenn Seaborg.[1][2] However, both this and other routes of synthesis of precious metals via nuclear reactions is orders of magnitude removed from economic viability.


Chlorine, sulfur and carbon (as coal) are cheapest by mass. Hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine are cheapest by volume at atmospheric pressure.


</fragment>

content:
**The four chemical elements that regularly top the “price‑per‑gram” lists** (mostly because they are either extremely rare naturally or can only be made in tiny amounts in a nuclear laboratory) are:

| Rank | Element (most common isotope used for pricing) | Approx. price / gram* | Year of discovery | Discoverer(s) |
|------|-----------------------------------------------|----------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | **Californium‑252** (a synthetic trans‑uranic radio‑isotope) | ≈ US $27 million / g (the highest quoted commercial price) | **1950** | Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg and co‑workers at the University of California, Berkeley |
| 2 | **Astatine‑210** (the longest‑lived astatine isotope, also synthetic) | ≈ US $100 million / g (estimated; only micro‑gram quantities have ever been produced) | **1940** | Dale R. Corson, K. R. MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè (at UC Berkeley) |
| 3 | **Francium‑223** (the most stable francium isotope) | ≈ US $10 million / g (estimated; only a few atoms ever isolated) | **1939** | Marguerite Perey (Paris) |
| 4 | **Lutetium** (the rarest of the stable lanthanides) | ≈ US $10 000 / g (bulk market price for high‑purity metal) | **1907** | Georges Urbain (France) – independently also discovered by Carl Auer von Welsbach (Austria) |

\* **Price notes**  
* Prices are taken from the most recent publicly quoted figures (typically from the *Prices of chemical elements* Wikipedia page, recent market reports, and specialist supplier quotations).  
* For the synthetic radio‑isotopes (californium‑252, astatine‑210, francium‑223) the quoted price reflects the cost of producing a **micro‑gram** or **nanogram** batch in a high‑flux nuclear reactor or particle accelerator; the price per gram is therefore an extrapolation that illustrates just how scarce and expensive they are.  
* Lutetium is the most expensive **stable** element that can be bought in macroscopic quantities; its price is driven by the difficulty of separating it from other rare‑earth metals.

### Why these four are at the top

| Element | Reason for extreme cost |
|---------|--------------------------|
| **Californium‑252** | Produced only in specialized reactors; each gram requires many weeks of irradiation of plutonium targets and costly chemical separation. Its high neutron‑emission rate makes it valuable for neutron‑radiography, oil‑well logging, and nuclear‑reactor start‑up, which keeps demand (and price) high. |
| **Astatine‑210** | No stable isotopes; the longest‑lived (8‑hour) isotope is made by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles. The production yield is minuscule (nanograms per week) and the element decays quickly, so any larger quantity would be prohibitively expensive. |
| **Francium‑223** | The most stable isotope has a half‑life of only 22 minutes. It can be generated only as a decay product of actinium‑227 or by cyclotron reactions, yielding at most a few atoms at a time. The cost of the equipment and the ultra‑short handling time push the price into the millions per gram. |
| **Lutetium** | Although stable, it is the rarest of the lanthanides in the Earth’s crust (~0.5 ppm). Separation from other rare‑earths requires many solvent‑extraction steps and ion‑exchange processes, making high‑purity lutetium costly. It finds niche uses in PET‑scanner catalysts and high‑performance lasers, sustaining a relatively high market price. |

### Quick reference

| Element | Discovery year | Approx. price/gram |
|---------|----------------|--------------------|
| Californium‑252 | 1950 | $27 M |
| Astatine‑210 | 1940 | $100 M (estimated) |
| Francium‑223 | 1939 | $10 M (estimated) |
| Lutetium | 1907 | $10 k |

These figures illustrate how the combination of **synthetic production difficulty**, **extreme radio‑activity**, and **natural scarcity** drives the price of the world’s most expensive elements.
